newsitem.title: UK: European oil traders welcome IPE gas oil probe.
newsitem.headline: European oil traders welcome IPE gas oil probe.

text.p: European oil traders welcomed on Friday the announcement of an inquiry into the International Petroleum Exchange's (IPE) gas oil futures contract as a step towards preventing disruption arising from delivery problems.
"We are quite happy that finally we are going to have someone look at this," a Scandinavian trader said.

"The November delivery was a screw-up. I really don't give a damn who was to blame, but that sort of thing could kill the IPE," he added, referring to a highly-charged dispute between the long and the short over the November delivery.
A trader in Switzerland: "This move should have been done a long time ago ... If we had enforcement rules like they have on the Merc (NYMEX) that would ensure a more orderly contract."

The IPE said on Thursday it had appointed British energy consultant Sally Clubley to carry out an independent review of the contract after what it called recent "strains", in particular difficulties with delivery.
An IPE statement said it expected the review to be completed by mid-March and anticipated Clubley would look at the way similar contracts were handled in the United States.

Clubley told Reuters on Thursday she would talk to U.S. market traders, among other industry players, to help formulate possible reforms of Europe's main winter energy market. She suggested she would look in particular at enforcement.
"I'll certainly talk to NYMEX (the New York Mercantile Exchange), and to traders who trade both NYMEX and the IPE, as well as those who just trade one (market)," Clubley told Reuters.

"There is a feeling that it may not be so much the rules (that are at issue) so much as the enforcement of the rules. People do feel the exchanges do operate very differently. In a time of very regulated markets there may be grounds for looking at this," she said.

A trader in London said: "I'm sceptical about how far you can control a market simply through regulation. I don't believe you can find a formula that alone will correct that situation. But if they want to strengthen enforcement, then that is good. Let's wait and see what is decided."
But a German importer was more critical, saying without elaborating: "I don't think this is enough. That's all I want to say".
The IPE said that in the event that Clubley recommended any changes, it expected to introduce such changes before the end of 1997.

The IPE made no mention of a showdown over the November delivery between AIC and Cargill that triggered criticism by European oil traders of the conduct of the continent's main winter oil market. Traders said the duel paralysed much of the Rotterdam oil barge market.
Some have called for tighter contract terms. Others have called for tougher fines, expressing admiration for NYMEX's practice of big spot fines for misbehaviour.
Clubley, a biochemist and former oil trader who lectures at the College of Petroleum and Energy Studies at Oxford, said she would not be probing the AIC-Cargill standoff.
"This (inquiry) is the future, not the past. The IPE has all the procedures in place (to handle the AIC-Cargill affair)," she said.
